subtype: Selling with fake reviews and testimonials [Observer]
passage: In the tailoring shop she ran in the kasba, Rajni looked over Sunaina's shoulder at the phone. Sunaina wanted to order a sewing machine motor from a shopping page. "Five stars, see? Three hundred reviews!" Rajni scrolled. "Best product, very nice, fast delivery." "Best product, very nice, fast delivery." The same words again and again, under different names. Not one review below four stars. "Strange," Rajni said. "Even Mishra-ji's sweets get complaints, and his are the best in the district." She tapped the filter for three-star reviews. Nothing, as if they had been hidden. Then she searched the motor's name in the tailors' group Sunaina's cousin had added them to. Two women from Rewa had bought it: it burned out in a month, and the seller stopped answering. Sunaina put the phone down slowly. "I almost ordered it tonight." "Ask the group which one they use," Rajni said, threading her needle. "Real people grumble a bit."

qa.q: Which words appeared again and again in the reviews?
qa.a: Best product, very nice, fast delivery.

qa.q: What was Rajni thinking as she scrolled?
qa.a: Rajni felt suspicious and puzzled that every review used the same words and none was below four stars, when even the best sweets get complaints.

qa.q: Which checks would you advise before buying from a page like this?
qa.a: Look for middle-rated reviews, notice identical wording, and ask independent people, like the tailors' group, who have really used the product.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel after hearing about the women from Rewa?
qa.a: Sunaina felt shaken and relieved, putting the phone down slowly as she realised she had almost ordered it that night.

grounding: Shows an adult noticing a page of identical glowing reviews with no complaints, and finding the truth through middle ratings and independent buyers.

passage: Zanele was on the minibus home in Johannesburg when the message landed in her class group: a blurry photo and the words, "Kids from Westridge High trashed our field last night. Share so everyone knows what they're like!" Her face went hot. Westridge had beaten them in the netball final and laughed about it. Of course it was them. Without a second look, she forwarded it to three more groups and added, "Typical." It felt good, like standing up for her school. By the time she got home it was everywhere. Then Rafael texted her: "That photo's from a news story two years ago, different city. My brother looked it up." Zanele stared at the screen. She hadn't even wondered where it came from. Her stomach dropped. She had wanted it to be true so badly. She typed into each group: "I shared this without checking. It's an old photo from somewhere else. Sorry."

qa.q: What did the message claim Westridge kids had done?
qa.a: Trashed their field last night.

qa.q: Why did forwarding the message feel good to Zanele?
qa.a: Zanele felt angry at Westridge after the netball final, and sharing felt loyal, like standing up for her school.

qa.q: What did Zanele do to repair it, and what could she do next time?
qa.a: She posted a correction in each group; next time she could ask where a photo came from before sharing, especially when it makes her angry.

qa.q: How might Westridge students feel about the message?
qa.a: They would likely feel hurt and unfairly blamed for something they didn't do, while the photo spread across many groups.

grounding: Shows a teenager forwarding a shocking message because it fits what her group already feels, without checking the source while angry.

subtype: Repeated claims begin to feel true [Receiver]
passage:
"Don't eat that," Maria said, pushing Jagdish's plate away. "The new contractor puts chemicals in everything. Everyone knows."
"Everyone who?"
"It's on every group. There were posters in the hostel. Sreeja said it, the seniors said it, it's literally everywhere."
"Okay. But what's the proof?"
Maria opened her mouth. Closed it. "It's just obvious. They're new, they're cutting costs."
"Did anyone test the food? Did anyone get sick?"
"I heard about some guy."
"Which guy?"
"I don't know his name." Maria frowned. "Wait. I've heard it so many times I stopped asking."
Jagdish shrugged. "I've eaten here every day for a month. And the old contractor's cousin runs the shop outside the gate. He printed those posters."
Maria stared at her samosa. "So I've been angry at these people for three weeks because of posters."
"Want to ask the student council to get the food checked? Then we'll actually know."

qa.q: Who printed the posters, according to Jagdish?
qa.a: The old contractor's cousin, who runs the shop outside the gate.

qa.q: What did Maria realise about her own certainty?
qa.a: Maria felt uneasy and a bit foolish, seeing that the claim had been heard so many times that asking for proof had stopped.

qa.q: What sensible step does Jagdish suggest?
qa.a: Asking the student council to get the food checked, so the claim is tested instead of just repeated.

qa.q: How might the new contractor be affected by the claim?
qa.a: The contractor could lose customers and be blamed without any proof, harmed by repetition alone.

grounding: Shows a young adult who came to accept a repeated claim about a clear villain as obvious, without any proof.

passage: On Monday, at the handpump, Seema heard it first: Hemant, the new compounder at the health sub-centre, was keeping some of the free medicines. By Wednesday, on the temple steps, it had grown: he sold them in town. By Friday, in the women's group, someone said he had been caught, and a mother said she would not take her child to him anymore. Seema, who taught at the village primary school, had seen Hemant carry medicines on his cycle to houses in the rain. She asked each person the same question: "Who told you?" Each named someone else. Nobody had seen anything. On Saturday she walked to the sub-centre. Hemant's eyes were red. "Two families didn't bring their babies for vaccination this week," he said quietly. "Nobody has even asked me." Seema sat down. "Then let's ask the ANM to show the stock register at the panchayat meeting, in front of everyone."

qa.q: What had the rumour grown into by Wednesday?
qa.a: That Hemant sold the medicines in town.

qa.q: What was Seema feeling as the rumour grew?
qa.a: Seema felt uneasy and doubtful, remembering Hemant carrying medicines in the rain, and troubled that nobody had seen anything.

qa.q: What makes Seema's next step wise?
qa.a: Showing the stock register at the panchayat meeting tests the rumour with facts, in front of the same people who spread it.

qa.q: How has the rumour affected Hemant and the village?
qa.a: Hemant is hurt, his eyes red, and two families skipped their babies' vaccinations, so harm came before anyone asked who first said it.

grounding: Shows a neighbour watching a rumour about a health worker grow from group to group and cause harm before anyone asks who first said it.

passage: The mehendi was loud, the dhol thumping, and Simran's phone was at four per cent when the forward reached her colony group: a shaky voice note warning that child-lifters in disguise were roaming the area, "share with every parent NOW". Around her, aunties were already forwarding. Reena, her cousin, grabbed her arm. "Send it to your building group! Their kids play outside." Simran's thumb hovered. Her own heart was racing. Then she made herself ask the questions her journalism professor used to drill. Who made this? No name. Where? No place. Why? To make me too scared to think. And who gets hurt if it's wrong? Any poor stranger walking past a frightened crowd. "I'm not sending it," she said. "Not till someone checks." Reena stared. "What if it's true?" "Then the police will know. Call the station from your phone and ask." Reena did. The duty officer said there were no such reports and asked people to stop forwarding.

qa.q: How much battery did Simran's phone have?
qa.a: Four per cent.

qa.q: How did Simran feel when the forward arrived?
qa.a: Simran felt scared, her heart racing, and tempted to forward it like everyone else.

qa.q: Which questions helped Simran decide?
qa.a: Who made it, where it happened, why it wanted her scared, and who gets hurt if it is wrong; with no answers, she held back and had the police asked.

qa.q: What might happen to a stranger if the voice note kept spreading?
qa.a: An innocent stranger could be surrounded and harmed by a frightened crowd, based on nothing.

grounding: Shows a person asking who made a frightening message and whether it aims to scare, and refusing to forward it unchecked amid pressure.

passage:
Tuesday
This morning a voice note went round the class group: Sumit's voice, calling Mrs D'Souza names I won't write here. It was so clearly him, the way he says "basically", the little laugh. I believed it straight away. I even sent an angry reply.
At break Sumit was white as chalk. He said he never said it, and he was shaking. I didn't believe him at first. Then he showed our class teacher, and Mr Ansari played it on the laptop, slowed down. There were odd gaps, and one word sounded pasted in. He said voices can be copied now from old clips, and videos too. By lunch he had taken it to the principal, asked the group admin to delete it, and told us all to stop sharing.
I feel awful. I heard it with my own ears, and my ears were wrong. From now on, hearing isn't proof. I owe Sumit an apology. Not tomorrow. I'm messaging him now.
Rajni

qa.q: What did Mr Ansari do with the voice note?
qa.a: He played it on the laptop, slowed down.

qa.q: How does Rajni feel after learning the note was fake?
qa.a: Rajni feels awful and guilty for believing it and sending an angry reply, shaken that even one's own ears can be wrong.

qa.q: What will Rajni do now, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Rajni is apologising to Sumit right away and will no longer treat audio or video as proof by itself, which stops adding to the harm.

qa.q: What was the morning like for Sumit?
qa.a: Sumit was white and shaking, accused of words he never said and not believed at first by classmates.

grounding: Shows a teenager who believed a faked voice note of a classmate because it sounded real, learning that the medium itself is no longer proof.

subtype: Why people make and share fakes [Observer]
passage:
Monday: Rashmi watched her cousin forward a video of a shark swimming down a flooded city street. Rashmi noticed it had no date or place, but said nothing.
Wednesday: In media class, Ms Sonali played the same clip. "It's edited. Old footage, somewhere else. So why would anyone make it?" Hands went up. "Money, from views." "Just to trick people." "To make one side look bad." Ms Sonali nodded. "And why do your aunties share it?" Silence. "Because it feels true. They're scared of floods, so a scary video fits. They're not lying; they believe it."
Saturday: At a family lunch, Rashmi's Mama forwarded a clip about a "poisoned" festival sweet. Rashmi didn't roll her eyes this time. "Mama, who do you think made this? And what would they get from it?" He paused, then laughed. "Views, I suppose." He didn't forward it again.

qa.q: What reasons did students give for making fakes?
qa.a: Money from views, to trick people, and to make one side look bad.

qa.q: How did Rashmi seem to feel at the family lunch, compared with Monday?
qa.a: Rashmi seemed calmer and more confident, asking Mama questions instead of staying silent or rolling her eyes.

qa.q: Why does asking about motive help?
qa.a: Asking who made it and what they would gain lets people doubt calmly without feeling accused, as happened with Mama.

qa.q: Why might Rashmi's Mama have forwarded the clip in the first place?
qa.a: He probably felt it was true or worrying rather than wanting to lie, just as Ms Sonali said about the aunties.

grounding: Shows a teacher explaining that fakes are made for money, clicks, politics or cruelty and shared by people who believe them, and a teen using that to doubt calmly.

subtype: Deepfake used to shame or extort [Receiver]
passage: I'm Dolma, and I'm telling this on your podcast, Anand, because last year I thought my life was over. A message came from an unknown account: a picture with my face, my hostel room behind me, but a body that wasn't mine. "Pay by Friday or this goes to your family and your college group." I was shaking so hard I dropped the phone. My first thought was, it's my fault for posting my photos. It wasn't. Someone took ordinary pictures and faked the rest. My roommate Pema made me do three things that same night. We saved everything: screenshots, the account name, the payment details they sent. We reported the account to the platform. And we went to the cyber police station together, where the officer said they see this every week and that I must not pay. Then I called my elder sister. Telling her was the hardest part. She just said, "I'm with you."

qa.q: What did the message demand?
qa.a: Payment by Friday, or the picture would go to Dolma's family and college group.

qa.q: What did Dolma first believe about whose fault it was?
qa.a: Dolma felt terrified and ashamed, first thinking it was Dolma's own fault for posting photos.

qa.q: What steps did Dolma and Pema take that night?
qa.a: They saved all the evidence, reported the account to the platform and went to the cyber police station without paying; then Dolma called an elder sister.

qa.q: How did Dolma's sister respond, and why did it matter?
qa.a: The sister simply said “I'm with you”, meeting the hardest moment with support instead of blame.

grounding: Shows a young person targeted with a faked image and a demand for money, learning it is not their fault, and saving evidence, reporting and telling family.

passage:
"Chinmay, look. The flyover near the station collapsed this morning!" Maria pushed her phone across the breakfast table.
"Hang on." He watched it twice. "Where does it say that?"
"The caption. Our city, today, share fast."
"Who posted it first?"
"Some page called City Alerts 24."
"Let's see what the local news sites say." He searched. "Nothing. Not one of them. A flyover falling would be everywhere."
"Maybe it just happened."
"Maybe. But look at the buses. Red double-deckers. Ours are green." He paused the frame. "And the shop signs aren't in any language we read here."
Maria leaned closer. "Okay, that's weird."
He ran an image search on one frame. "Here. Same video, another country, three years ago."
"So it's real, just not here."
"Real clip, wrong story. And if I couldn't find anything either way, I still wouldn't share it."
Maria deleted the forward she'd half-typed to her office group.

qa.q: What colour are the buses in their city?
qa.a: Green.

qa.q: What made Maria stop before forwarding?
qa.a: Maria felt alarmed at first, then puzzled and doubtful once Chinmay pointed out the red double-deckers and the unfamiliar shop signs.

qa.q: Which checks did Chinmay use?
qa.a: He asked who posted it first, searched local news sites, noticed odd details like the buses and signs, and ran an image search on a frame.

qa.q: What would change if Maria had forwarded it to her office group?
qa.a: Colleagues might panic or avoid the station, and a wrong story would spread further under Maria's name.

grounding: Shows an adult tracing a clip's original source, checking trusted outlets and odd details, and not sharing what cannot be checked.

Omkar: the ones from the basketball court?
Mridul: yeah. they're so nice. they said I'm one of them after 2 weeks. first time anyone here said that
Omkar: that's nice. it's been rough since you moved
Mridul: but today Varun bhaiya said real members don't hang out with outside people, and I shouldn't tell my parents about the meets. they "wouldn't understand"
Omkar: wait. hide it from your parents?
Mridul: he said it's a test of loyalty
Omkar: that's the bit that's off. a good group doesn't need you to hide it or drop me
Mridul: yeah. my stomach went weird when he said it
Omkar: tell your mum tonight? I'll come over if you want
Mridul: ok. telling her now
Mridul: she listened, said I did right to tell her and it's normal to want friends. I'm not going to the 5am thing, and she's calling the school counsellor first thing tomorrow
Omkar: good. basketball at 6 instead? just us

qa.q: How long had Mridul known the group when they said Mridul was one of them?
qa.a: Two weeks.

qa.q: Why is the Circle so appealing to Mridul?
qa.a: Mridul has felt lonely since moving, so being called one of them felt warm and welcoming for the first time.

qa.q: What was the key warning sign, and what did Mridul do about it?
qa.a: Being told to hide the meets from parents and drop outside friends; Mridul told Mum that same evening and is skipping the 5am meet.

qa.q: How does Omkar see the group?
qa.a: Omkar is glad Mridul has friends but worried about the secrecy and cutting-off, and offers support and company.

grounding: Shows a lonely teenager drawn to an intense group offering quick belonging, where pressure to hide it and drop others is the warning sign.
